statements.quote: We need a single payer, Medicare-for-all system in Massachusetts
statements.claim: Explicitly supports establishing single payer in Massachusetts, not just a national program.

statements.quote: NO. I support federal single payer
statements.claim: Opposes the Massachusetts-only single-payer proposal while explicitly supporting federal single payer; cites interstate coverage and MassHealth administration concerns.

statements.quote: end the ban on rent control
statements.claim: Emphasizes restoring municipal rent-control authority and public housing investment; also answers yes to transit-area multifamily housing.

statements.quote: The long-term solution is simple: build more housing.
statements.claim: Emphasizes more diverse, transit-oriented housing and subsidies, while also supporting tenant protections, municipal rent-stabilization authority and eviction counsel.

statements.quote: to make the State House the people’s house
statements.claim: Frames progressive taxation, public investment, grassroots organizing and legislative transparency as a way to reclaim state government from concentrated power.

statements.quote: reform the system from the inside out
statements.claim: Emphasizes changing institutional culture by listening, developing common goals and using evidence about program results.

statements.quote: a Medicare for All-type system at the state level
statements.claim: Supports Massachusetts single payer and organizing a statewide movement; explicitly also accepts incremental measures that improve access or affordability.

statements.quote: I support single payer health care
statements.claim: Explicitly supports state single payer and says she co-sponsors legislation for it; also proposes a MassHealth public-option buy-in as a step toward it.

statements.quote: I intend to build the movement across the state
statements.claim: Makes statewide movement-building for single payer the objective, while saying she would vote for useful incremental bills.

statements.quote: a public option, Masshealth buy-in program
statements.claim: Describes a public-option MassHealth buy-in as a route toward single payer, not a rejection of single payer.

statements.quote: social housing and community land trusts
statements.claim: Proposes social housing and land trusts alongside transfer fees, tenant protections and transit-area multifamily housing.

statements.quote: zone for multifamily housing
statements.claim: Emphasizes transit-area multifamily zoning, accessible housing, accessory units and tenant protections, including municipal rent-control authority.

statements.quote: movement building as my #1 priority
statements.claim: Makes expanding participation and building grassroots movements the leading strategy for legislative change.

statements.quote: keeping people with different goals working together
statements.claim: Emphasizes collaborative coalitions of legislators and outside advocates, with clear messaging and policy design.

statements.quote: right to counsel and rent stabilization
statements.claim: Explicitly proposes renter counsel and rent stabilization within a broader Homes Guarantee.

statements.quote: an idea that deserves consideration
statements.claim: Says rent control deserves consideration after robust public debate and comprehensive design; this is not an outright rejection.

statements.quote: rent-restricted or limited-equity properties to community land trusts
statements.claim: Would fund and authorize public acquisition and transfer of restricted-affordability homes to community land trusts.

statements.quote: Incentives to start and grow community land trusts
statements.claim: Proposes incentives to establish and expand community land trusts.

statements.quote: I support a ban on fracking.
statements.claim: Supports a fracking ban, linked to union brownfield-remediation jobs and investment in a clean-energy transition.

statements.quote: I would support a ban for now at least
statements.claim: Supports a ban at least while permitting and its integrity are evaluated, and describes a longer renewable-energy transition. He is not coded as categorically opposing a ban.

statements.quote: I support safe consumption sites
statements.claim: Supports supervised consumption sites within a treatment- and diversion-oriented response to substance use.

statements.quote: must have the support of their host community
statements.claim: Supports safe-injection and harm-reduction sites, explicitly requiring host-community dialogue and support before operation.

statements.quote: I support a push to enact a version of it here
statements.claim: Supports a Pennsylvania version of AB5 worker classification, with clearer negotiated professional-service exemptions.

statements.quote: Yes, I support AB5.
statements.claim: Supports AB5's approach and says staff are reviewing implementation for Pennsylvania.

statements.quote: $15 an hour as a floor
statements.claim: Proposes a minimum wage with a $15 hourly floor.

statements.quote: $12-15 an hour
statements.claim: Proposes increasing the wage to a stated $12-15 range and indexing it annually to inflation, without specifying an exact endpoint.

statements.quote: represent movement power in Harrisburg
statements.claim: Presents his campaign as a vehicle for labor and community movements in state government.

statements.quote: develop relationships with senators on the other side of the aisle
statements.claim: Emphasizes cross-party legislative relationships alongside winning Democratic majorities.

statements.quote: reintroduce a single healthcare payer bill
statements.claim: States support for reintroducing a Pennsylvania single-payer bill. No anti-single-payer assumption follows from his incumbent status.

statements.quote: a Green New Deal for schools
statements.claim: Proposes school toxin remediation alongside energy, cooling and other green-building upgrades.

comparisons.analysis: Uyterhoeven supports a Massachusetts single-payer system; Sharp explicitly answers no to that state-level proposal while supporting federal single payer. The disagreement must not be generalized into Sharp opposing single payer at every level.

Uyterhoeven foregrounds rent-control authority and public investment; Sharp foregrounds housing supply and transit-oriented development. Both also support tenant protections and transit-area multifamily housing, so these are not mutually exclusive platforms.
Uyterhoeven emphasizes grassroots accountability and changing who state government serves; Sharp emphasizes internal cultural reform, shared understandings and program evaluation.
Both explicitly support Massachusetts single payer. Barber's additional public-option proposal is described as a step toward it, not a repudiation of it.

Callahan emphasizes organizing a statewide single-payer movement; Barber names a MassHealth buy-in public option as an interim route. Callahan also says she accepts useful incremental bills, so this is not an uncompromising-versus-pragmatic binary.

Callahan foregrounds social housing and land trusts; Barber foregrounds zoning, accessibility and tenant protections. Both support tenant protections and housing production; omission is not opposition.
Callahan makes movement-building her leading governing strategy; Barber emphasizes legislative and advocacy coalitions that can pass policy. Both describe working with groups beyond the legislature.
Saval proposes rent stabilization directly; Farnese favors considering rent control after public debate and design work. The latter is a qualified deliberative position, not explicit opposition.
Both support community land trusts, with Saval specifying public acquisition and restricted-affordability transfers and Farnese proposing growth incentives.

Saval endorses a fracking ban linked to worker-transition programs. Farnese supports a ban at least during review of permitting. The difference is its stated duration and conditions, not a simple pro-/anti-ban split.

Both support supervised consumption sites; Farnese explicitly requires host-community support before operation. Saval's answer does not state that condition, but its absence is not proof he rejects community consultation.
Both support an AB5-style worker-classification law. Saval discusses negotiating clearer exemptions; Farnese says implementation is under review.
Saval specifies a $15 floor; Farnese gives a $12-15 range with inflation indexing. An exact Farnese endpoint or categorical rejection of $15 is not invented.
Saval emphasizes movement representation; Farnese emphasizes cross-party relationships and electing a Democratic majority. These are stated approaches, not measured effectiveness.
